title: The Invisible Infrastructure: Ensuring U.S. Federal Water Data Integrity and Continuity for a Non‐Stationary Future
content:
ABSTRACT

U.S. federal hydrologic datasets and modeling frameworks constitute a foundational public utility, essential for engineering resilient infrastructure in an era of non-stationarity, to maintain public safety and national security. However, recent institutional restructuring and funding shifts have created an unprecedented threat to this “invisible infrastructure.” This commentary examines the consequences of the declining U.S. Geological Survey National Streamgage Network, the administrative delays surrounding the rollout of NOAA Atlas 15, and the destabilization of integrated U.S. federal modeling centers like the National Center for Atmospheric Research. These are examples, but not the complete extent, of U.S. federal data loss and their resultant consequences. These U.S. federal resources fill a unique niche of high-rigor and perpetual observation that neither the commercial sector nor academia can replicate, and serve as a model that other national governments, especially in Europe, are emulating. Drawing on recent analyses of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Atlas 15 pilot data, we demonstrate that data erosion can lead to “policy blindness” at a time of large-scale investment in infrastructure upgrades and both compromised public safety and national security. To ensure a resilient future, the engineering profession requires unhindered access to timely, transparent, curated data that only the U.S. federal government can reliably provide.
